abstract: |
  A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.
keywords:
  - Reproducibility
  - Large Language Models (LLMs)
  - Data analysis decisions
  - Many-analysts study
  - Statistical workflow

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

<!-- , a gap also identified in prior work on authoring statistical models from conceptual relationships [@jun2022; @jun2022hypothesis].  -->

A data analysis is the product of a chain of decisions, from how the data are cleaned to how the model is specified. Those decisions are what a reader needs in order to comprehend an analysis, judge whether it is reasonable, and extend it by asking how the result would change under different choices. Standard practice in reproducible research [@peng_reproducible_2011; @wrobel_partnering_2024] asks for the code and the data to be made available, but does not extend to the decisions behind them.

The distinction arises because code and the decisions it implements operate at different levels: code specifies precisely what a computer should do, while a decision has a contextual interpretation that the code itself does not capture. Consider a line such as `dplyr::filter(df, x > 0)`, which has a precise meaning as code: keep rows where `x` is positive. Which decision this line encodes is not something the code can answer: it could represent restricting the analysis to a subpopulation for which $x > 0$ is substantively meaningful, or excluding observations flagged as invalid by an encoding convention where $x \le 0$ denotes missingness, and nothing in the `filter()` syntax indicates which is intended. Nor does code generally carry the rationale behind a decision, unless the author has left detailed comments. A better place to state the decisions is in the manuscript, where decisions are described along with their rationale. But this information is scattered across the manuscript rather than collected in one place, with preprocessing and modeling decisions appearing in different sections of the manuscript. Authors may also simply leave out decisions they consider minor, on the assumption that the code provides all the detail a reader would need. Reconstructing the full sequence, therefore, means searching across the paper and the code for decisions and their rationale before a reader can begin to comprehend the analysis. Ideally, this sequence of decisions and their rationale would live in a single file, so a reader can follow the analysis directly rather than piecing it together from multiple sources. This file should also be extensible, so a reader can specify an alternative decision and easily evaluate it to see how the result would change.

<!-- In other words, code and manuscript are complementary but each incomplete: the code is precise but mingled with implementation details and largely silent on rationale, while the manuscript carries rationale but scatters it across sections and sometimes omits it.  -->

<!-- What is needed is a representation that records each decision together with its rationale, in one place, so a reader can follow the analysis without parsing the code or piecing the rationale together from across the manuscript. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) make such a representation practical: LLMs now translate natural-language descriptions into executable code with considerable reliability [@jiang2026survey; @shah_automating_2026; @chen2021codex; @lai_ds1000_2023; @huang_executionbased_2022], so once a decision is described in a schema, an LLM can generate and validate the corresponding code directly from it. The same representation also makes extending an analysis easier. Data analysis is often underdetermined, with many plausible choices regarding data preprocessing, transformation, aggregation, and model specification [@gao_nonstandard_2026; @bertran_many_2026; @luo_can_2025], and a reader may reasonably want to know whether a conclusion would still hold under one of these other choices, for example, "What if we had included observations with $x \leq 0$?" This question motivates multiverse analysis [@steegen2016] and specification curve analysis [@simonsohn2020], which report a result across the set of defensible analytical choices rather than a single path through it. Because each decision is recorded explicitly rather than embedded in code, a reader can specify such an alternative directly and have it evaluated through the same schema and the same LLM-based translation into code, rather than modifying the original script by hand. -->

In this paper, we present a schema that records a data analysis as a sequence of decisions, each stated with the objective it addresses and the rationale for choosing it, together with the variables it consumes and produces. We also demonstrate how this schema, coupled with large language models (LLMs), can be used to generate code scripts from natural-language descriptions in manuscripts, and explore alternative decision choices. We present two applications. The first takes the perspective of an author supplying a schema alongside a published manuscript, using the GAITD regression analysis of heaped smoking data in @yee2025heaping. A reader can then specify an alternative file, coupled with the original schema, to compare model performance under a different inflation-alteration specification. The second, the many-analysts football study, considers the opposite situation, where no schema is supplied and the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility test. It extracts a schema from a simplified version of each team's report, generates and validates the corresponding code, and compares the result against that team's published estimate. Of the six teams whose reported estimates we do not recover, three trace to reports that do not describe the analysis precisely enough to regenerate it, including one whose text names a different covariate from its own results table. We further demonstrate how the schema supports specification and exploration of three alternative random effect structures for Team 5.

The paper is organized as follows: In @sec-method, we present our methodology, including the schema representation for describing data analysis, the specification of the alternative file, and the workflow for generating and validating code from the schema with LLMs. In @sec-gaitd, we construct a schema for a published GAITD regression analysis and show how it allows a reader to evaluate an alternative specification directly. In @sec-application, we apply the workflow as a reproducibility test to the many-analysts football study, recovering the reported results for most teams and discussing the failed cases. Finally, in @sec-discussion, we discuss the implications of our work and potential future directions.

The reproducibility movement has been a major development in modern scientific research, motivated in part by concerns regarding the replication of published findings and the increasing reliance on computational methods across disciplines. While these developments have improved the ability to reproduce computational results, they are not designed to make analyses easier to understand. Reproducibility concerns whether a result can be regenerated given the data, code, and computational environment, whereas comprehension concerns whether the audience can reconstruct the analytical decisions made by the authors, understand the rationale behind those decisions, and confidently modify the code to explore alternative choices. # Methodology {#sec-method}

## A schema for describing data analysis {#sec-schema}

We represent a data analysis, $\mathcal{S} = \{A_1, A_2, \cdots, A_n\}$, as a sequence of $n$ analysis decisions $A_i$, applied to a dataset $\mathcal{D}$, where each step, $A_i$, is defined as a tuple:

\begin{equation}
A_{i} = \langle f_{i}, \pi_{i}, \rho_{i}, \mathcal{I}_{i}, \mathcal{O}_{i}, \omega_{i} \rangle.
\end{equation}


$f_{i} \in \mathcal{F}$ is the *objective* of a step, identifying the problem the *decision*, $\pi_{i} \in \Pi$, is trying to solve. $\rho_{i}$ is the *rationale* provided for choosing the decision $\pi_{i}$. All three fields are written in short natural language sentences, and together they form a self-contained account of each decision in the analysis. As an example, @lst-schema presents the schema that describes the steps for calculating the Human Development Index (HDI) [@hdi]:

  1) Scale all four variables (life expectancy, expected years of schooling, mean years of schooling, and GNI per capita) to the [0, 1] range.
  2) Combine the two education variables (expected years of schooling and mean years of schooling) into a single education variable.
  3) Combine the three dimensions (health, education, and income) into a single index using a geometric mean. 

:::{#lst-schema lst-cap="An example schema for calculating Human Development Index (HDI)"}
````yaml
meta:
  type: schema
nodes:
- id: step-scaling
  objective: how to handle variables in different scales?
  decision: apply min-max scaling to each variable
  rationale: to convert the variables to the same scale for future
    construction of a single index
- id: step-education
  objective: how to combine the two education-related variables?
  decision: take the average
  rationale: the arithmetic mean allows perfect substitutability
    between the two variables
- id: step-combine
  objective: how to combine the three dimensions into a single index?
  decision: use the geometric mean
  rationale: the geometric mean penalizes uneven development 
    among the three core dimensions
````
:::

In the file, the `meta` field at the top marks the document as a schema (`type: schema`), and `nodes` below it records the analysis as a list of steps. Each step carries an `id` that names it, together with the `objective`, `decision`, and `rationale` fields holding $f_i$, $\pi_i$, and $\rho_i$. For instance, the objective of step 3 is to combine the three dimensions to create a single index. The geometric mean (the decision) is chosen over a simple arithmetic mean (an alternative, introduced in @sec-alternative) because it penalizes uneven development among the three dimensions (the rationale). 

Generating code from the schema also requires each step to be tied to concrete variables in the data. Where a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ is available, $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{O}_i$ record that mapping as part of the schema, so that it is fixed in advance rather than inferred at the point of code generation. Because the schema specifies an analysis before its code exists, $\mathcal{O}_i$ may name a variable that is not yet in the dataset. In contrast, $\mathcal{I}_i$ must already be in scope, comprising variables in the original dataset together with the outputs of all previous steps:

$$\mathcal{I}_{i} \subseteq \left( \mathcal{D} \cup \bigcup_{j < i} \mathcal{O}_{j} \right), \quad \forall i \in \{2, \dots, n\}.$$

<!-- In practice it most often names a new column added to the evolving dataset through non-standard evaluation, as in `tidyverse`-style pipelines. -->

A schema can be written by hand, or drafted by an LLM from an existing description of the analysis, such as the methodology section of a manuscript. In the latter case, $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{O}_i$ are inferred by the model whenever a dataset is provided, and each step carries a categorical confidence score, $\omega_{i}$ (low, medium, high), defined as the model's confidence that the recorded $(f_i, \pi_i, \rho_i)$ correctly reflects the source text. 

## Describing alternatives {#sec-alternative}

Recording a step's decision $\pi_i$ does not mean it is the only one that could satisfy its objective $f_i$: a reader may want to revisit the decision made for some of these steps and consider alternatives that address the same objective, the premise of multiverse analysis [@steegen2016; @simonsohn2020]. Formally, a step in the schema can have a candidate set of alternatives: step $i$ may admit $k_i$ decisions that all satisfy its objective $f_i$, $\{A_i^1, \dots, A_i^{k_i}\}$, of which the decision $\pi_i$ recorded in the schema is just one member, $A_i^1$. An alternative file specifies the remaining candidates, $A_i^2, \dots, A_i^{k_i}$, for a subset of steps $C \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$. 

The overall structure of an alternative file is shown in @lst-alternatives-skeleton. The `meta` field at the top identifies the file as an alternative specification (`type: alternatives`), and the file-level `branch` field, either `single` or `multi`, determines how the candidates at each step are combined. The `nodes` field then holds one entry for every step in $C$. Each entry uses `overrides` to name the step it applies to in the original schema, then lists that step's alternative decisions and their rationale.

:::{#lst-alternatives-skeleton lst-cap="The skeleton of an alternative YAML file, which consists of a `branch` mode and a list of covered steps."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: single | multi
nodes:
  - overrides: <step id>
    alternatives:
      - id: <alternative id>
        decision: <...>
        rationale: <...>
      - id: <alternative id>
        ...
  - overrides: <step id>
    alternatives:
      ...
  ...
````
:::

Under `branch: single`, every step is restricted to a single candidate decision. These alternatives, together with the rest of the original schema, form one new analysis. This is useful when an analyst already has a specific alternative analysis in mind and wants to evaluate it as a whole. @lst-alternatives-single fills in the skeleton to construct an alternative HDI computation, using a harmonic mean to combine the two education variables in Step 2 and an arithmetic mean to combine the three dimensions in Step 3.

:::{#lst-alternatives-single lst-cap="A sample alternative file that changes the decisions for Step 2 and Step 3 in calculating Human Development Index (HDI)."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: single
nodes:
  - overrides: step-education
    alternatives:
      - id: harmonic-mean
        decision: take the harmonic mean of the two education variables
        rationale: penalizes disparity between the two schooling measures
          rather than allowing one to compensate for the other
  - overrides: step-combine
    alternatives:
      - id: arith-mean
        decision: use an arithmetic mean
        rationale: a simple average of the three dimensions
````
:::

Sometimes a reader instead wants to test a range of alternatives for one or more steps independently. Under `branch: multi`, each covered step may take any of its alternatives or keep its original decision, and every such combination across steps becomes a separate analysis. In @lst-alternatives-multi, one alternative is specified for the education step and two for the combination step. Together with the original schema, this produces $(1+1) \times (2+1) = 6$ analyses. More generally, with $k_i$ candidates at each step $i \in C$, crossing all candidates yields $\prod_{i \in C} k_i$ analyses.
  
:::{#lst-alternatives-multi lst-cap="A sample alternative file that explores one alternative decision for Step 2 and two for Step 3 in calculating Human Development Index (HDI). Combining these alternatives with the original schema produces a total of (1+1) × (2+1) = 6 analyses."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: multi
nodes:
  - overrides: step-education
    alternatives:
      - id: harmonic-mean
        decision: take the harmonic mean of the two education variables
        rationale: penalizes disparity between the two schooling measures
          rather than allowing one to compensate for the other
  - overrides: step-combine
    alternatives:
      - id: arith-mean
        decision: use an arithmetic mean
        rationale: a simple average of the three dimensions
      - id: min-agg
        decision: use the minimum of the three dimensions
        rationale: a "weakest-link" aggregation that penalizes any single
          lagging dimension more strongly than an average would
````
:::

Existing multiverse tooling, such as the `multiverse` package in R [@sarma2023], expresses each branch in code, while our alternatives are instead specified at the level of decisions, in natural language, from which modern LLMs can generate the corresponding code. Keeping them in a separate file also changes who can pose the alternative question: a multiverse is conventionally built by the original analyst exploring their own garden of forking paths, whereas an alternative file can be written by a reader after reading the published manuscript, against a schema the author has already supplied, to investigate questions that interest them. 

## Workflow {#sec-workflow}

The reliability of the generated code depends primarily on the quality of the schema. A schema that faithfully records the decisions of an analysis, in the form set out in @sec-schema, leaves little to be interpreted at the code generation stage, since the objective and the decision at each step are stated explicitly. The errors that remain are in the code implementation rather than the analysis: a missing `library()` call, or a misnamed function argument.

The validation stage is designed to resolve errors of this kind. The validation agent executes the script in a sandbox environment and, when execution fails, receives the script together with the error message and the line number at which it occurred, and returns a revised script. The revised script is then executed again, and the cycle continues until the script completes without error, a maximum number of attempts is reached, or the user terminates the process. Application to the many-analysts football study in @sec-application shows that this procedure resolves most of the syntax errors that arise in data wrangling and statistical modeling.

The same generation-validation procedure applies to multiple analyses. When a schema is augmented with an alternative file, the expansion described in @sec-alternative produces one schema for each combination of decisions, and each resulting schema is passed through the same generation and validation procedure independently.
 
@fig-workflow gives an overview of the workflow, which provides two paths for using a schema. Passing a schema through the code generation and validation stages produces a script whose execution yields the estimates of the analysis, which can be compared with the estimates originally reported, serving as a reproducibility check. A schema can also be augmented with an alternative file, expanding it into a multiverse of parallel analyses, so that the author and subsequent readers can explore the reported result under different decisions. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-workflow
#| out.width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: "Overview of the schema-driven analysis workflow. Schemas can be authored manually or generated from natural language manuscripts by an LLM. Schemas are used to generate code, which is validated through iterative execution in a sandboxed environment and repaired when errors occur. Alternative specifications can expand a schema into a multiverse of parallel analyses."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/workflow.png"))
```

We now analyze the uncertainty of the pipeline itself: for a step $k$ extracted by a model $M$ from a source text $T$, we decompose the total uncertainty of the pipeline at that step into a specification term and an implementation term,

$$V_k^{\text{total}}(M) = V_k^{\text{spec}}(M) + V_k^{\text{impl}}(M),$$

where each component is defined as the expected pairwise divergence, $d(\cdot, \cdot) \in [0, 1]$, between independent runs at the corresponding stage. Specifically, $V_k^{\text{spec}}(M)$ measures variation across repeated schema extractions from $T$ and $V_k^{\text{impl}}(M)$ measures variation across repeated code generations from a single fixed schema. We can further decompose the specification term into an epistemic and an aleatoric component [@kendall2017; @hullermeier2021]:

$$V_k^{\text{spec}}(M) = V_k^{\text{epistemic}}(M) + V_k^{\text{aleatoric}},$$

The epistemic component, $V_k^{\text{epistemic}}(M)$, reflects when the model fails to recover a decision that is unambiguously specified in  $T$. The aleatoric component, $V_k^{\text{aleatoric}}$, captures the uncertainty in the source itself: the text $T$ is unclear at step $k$, independent of $M$. This distinction has a direct diagnostic use in the quality of the data anlaysis. Persistent dispersion across increasingly capable models suggests that the observed variation reflects ambiguity in the source since a more capable model cannot recover the authors' intent that is not sufficiently expressed in the source text.

# Application: GAITD regression of heaped smoking data {#sec-gaitd}

In this section we demonstrate the workflow in the case where an author provides a faithful schema alongside a published manuscript, which a reader can then use to question and explore the analysis, following the second path in @fig-workflow. We use @yee2025heaping's GAITD regression analysis of heaped smoking data, published in the Annals of Applied Statistics, as the example. @yee2025heaping report four separate smoking-related responses, and for demonstration purposes, we build the schema for only the first response, smoking initiation age (P1, Section 5.1 of their paper). The same workflow extends to the other three cases.

The schema in @lst-heaping comprises fourteen entries, each recording an *objective*, a *decision*, and a *rationale* in the structure introduced in @sec-schema. Consider `special_value_mid_risk`: the decision is to treat ages 12-14 and 19-21 as one inflated group with extra probability mass, since these ages show a moderate, secondary peak in the spikeplots with the high-risk group (ages 15-18) showing the most prominent peak. Recording the rationale along with the decision allows a reader to agree or disagree with the authors' choice, and to question and explore the analysis, as we do later in this section.

:::{#lst-heaping lst-cap="A schema for the GAITD regression analysis of smoking initiation age in @yee2025heaping, constructed from the manuscript and intended to be provided alongside it as a self-contained account of the analysis."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/schema_draft.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

Assembling the schema does not require additional analysis from the authors, only the collection of decisions and rationale already present in the manuscript and supplementary material. 


<!-- required no analysis the authors had not already done, but it did require collecting the decisions from two documents and, in places, from code alone. Five of the fourteen appear nowhere in the manuscript. The manuscript records that cases with missing values in the adjustment variables were deleted and that the sample was restricted to respondents under 80; it does not record that `TC30`, `TCquit`, and `SCA` are exempt from that completeness check, that `SCA` and `SIA` are set to missing wherever `SCA - SIA < 0`, that marital status and education are overwritten by age for respondents under 20, or the two-branch rule that defines the ever-smoker sample. Each of these survives only as executable code in the supplementary material, and their stated rationale, where there is one, is a code comment: the completeness exemption is explained by the remarks that the variables are "interlaced with NAs" and that a missing value "means not yet quit, which is okay", the ever-smoker rule by the comment "Complex to handle NAs", and the data-quality correction by the single word "Bad". The two recodings carry no comment at all; a reader must infer their purpose from a note several pages later, written for another purpose, observing that marital status, education, and smoking initiation age "were not measured in those aged 19 or less". Recovering these decisions is exactly the piecing-together the schema is meant to remove, and it is worth emphasising that @yee2025heaping's supplementary material is unusually thorough as it walks through the analysis in a tutorial style, states general modelling guidelines upfront, and discusses competing options it rejected.  -->

As a check that this schema is accurate, generating and validating code from it produces the R script in @lst-script-sia, which reproduces the coefficients reported in Table 2 of @yee2025heaping. Since the code was generated without access to the manuscript or the authors' script, the match shows that the schema records everything needed to reproduce the analysis. A schema of this kind could therefore accompany a manuscript as reproducibility material in its own right, alongside code and data, and a reader can rely on it as an accurate account of the analysis it documents.

:::{#lst-script-sia lst-cap="The R script generated and validated from the schema in @lst-heaping, annotated with the `id` of the schema step each block implements."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````r\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/script_iter1_annotated.R")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

@yee2025heaping's supplementary material reports an investigation from a reviewer, who suggested splitting the mid-risk group into two, keeping ages 12-14 as inflated but treating ages 19-21 as altered instead, since that older subgroup shows a qualitatively different, declining pattern of uptake. @lst-ap1921 encodes the reviewer's suggestion as an alternative file, overriding three steps at once: `special_value_mid_risk` narrows the inflated group to ages 12-14, `alteration_operator_decision` turns on an alteration group for ages 19-21, and `covariate_selection` drops to an intercept-only model, matching how the authors themselves computed AIC for this comparison; `branch: single` ties the three overrides into one refit, rather than crossing them into separate branches. Generating and validating code from this alternative file reproduces the AIC of 19,340.4 that @yee2025heaping reports. Here the question was answered because the authors chose to report the refit in their supplement; with the schema available, any reader who raises such a question can answer it directly. 

:::{#lst-ap1921 lst-cap="An alternative YAML file specifying a joint change to the mid-risk inflation, alteration, and covariate steps in the GAITD schema, treating ages 19-21 as an alteration group rather than pooling them into the mid-risk inflated group."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/alt_ap1921.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::


# Application: many-analysts football study {#sec-application}

@sec-gaitd assumed the authors supply a schema alongside the manuscript, but a schema need not come from the authors. Since it records decisions in natural language, the schema can be extracted from the manuscript itself by an LLM for readers to understand and explore the analysis. In this section, we demonstrate the workflow in the opposite situation, where no schema is supplied and the workflow serves as a reproducibility test using the many-analysts football study [@silberzahn2018].

@silberzahn2018 invited 29 research groups to conduct the same data analysis, answering whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players than to light-skin-toned players. The provided dataset contains two raters' skin color ratings of players' pictures, the aggregated number of red cards received by a player from a referee across all matches in that player-referee pair, and other relevant player, referee, and game characteristics: player birthday, height, weight, player position, league country, number of victories, ties, and defeats. 

Each team was free to choose their own analysis approach; we take Team 5 as an illustration. They disaggregated the player-referee records into player–game observations, giving a binary response for whether a player received a red card, and removed incomplete cases by list-wise deletion. They then fitted a binomial generalized linear mixed model with a logit link, taking the average of the two raters' skin color ratings as the covariate of interest, with random intercepts for players and referees and a random intercept and slope for the referee's country of origin.

Team 5's analysis is only one of the approaches taken: other teams made different preprocessing decisions, assumed different distributions (linear, logistic, or Poisson), specified different fixed and random effects, or worked in a Bayesian framework. Each team was required to document its analysis in a report with a publishable methodology section. All of these are available on the Open Science Framework.

These reports are not directly usable as input since the many-analysts study also takes in a second research question and the construction of confidence intervals. Some teams write their final analysis as a set of edits to the initial one rather than as a self-contained methodology section. We therefore pre-extract a simplified methodology text for each team and use it in place of the report. 

Each team's text is then passed through the workflow of @sec-method to extract the schema and then generate and validate the corresponding code with Claude Opus 4.5. The Appendix follows Team 5 through the pipeline to show the input text, the schema, and the generated script.

To accelerate the evaluation of each script, we manually replace the standard modeling functions with faster counterparts after the scripts are generated but before validation: `lm()`/`glm()` with `fixest::feols()`/`fixest::feglm()` [@fixest], and `lme4::glmer()` [@lme4] with `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` [@glmmTMB-1]. These fit the same models by faster means, using multi-threaded C++ and Template Model Builder (TMB) respectively, so the substitution changes how the coefficients are computed, not the coefficients themselves. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
# df <- read_csv(here::here("data/res.csv"))
# df |> count(validate_iter_n) |> knitr::kable()
```

Of the 29 teams, the analyses of four teams (Teams 7, 12, 17, and 18) are too computationally expensive to run inside an iterative validate-and-repair loop, regardless of whether the schema or generated code is correct: Team 7 specifies a Dirichlet process profile regression, Team 12 a zero-inflated Poisson regression, and Teams 17 and 18 MCMC-based hierarchical models. Hence we exclude these four teams from the evaluation, leaving 25 teams whose analyses we attempt to reproduce. Across the 25 teams we reproduce, all team scripts were successfully executed after the validation phase. Notably, two scripts ran successfully without any validation, whereas the vast majority reached completion after two or three iterations. The most frequent correction involved resolving broken and overflowing syntax in comments. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-res-schema
#| out.width: 90%
#| out.height: 80%
#| fig.cap: "Comparison of the odds ratio of the effect of skin color on receiving red cards in football games from our schema-based reproduction (reproduced) vs. the effect size reported in @silberzahn2018 (reported). Teams are ordered by the absolute difference between the reproduced and reported odds ratio. The reproduction recovers the reported odds ratio closely for most teams; the largest deviations occur for Team 1, 9, 15, 21, 23, and 27."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/res-schema.png"))
```

@fig-res-schema shows the comparison of the estimated effect sizes, in odds ratio, from our schema workflow (reproduced) and those reported in @silberzahn2018 (reported). The odds ratio is well recovered for most teams, though six show a noticeably larger gap: Teams 1, 9, 15, 21, 23, and 27.

For Teams 1 and 23 the discrepancy originates in our code generation. When reshaping the data from the player-referee level to the game level, the schema correctly specifies this step, but the generated code fails to execute it as intended, and the resulting error passes through validation silently rather than triggering a repair.
<!-- The confidence score $\omega_i$ separates these two cases in a way worth noting. For Team 27, extraction returned `create_interaction_terms` with medium confidence, flagging the step whose reading is in doubt before any code was written. For Team 9, every step came back with high confidence, which is the correct response rather than an oversight: the report's text is unambiguous on its own terms, and the inconsistency appears only when that text is set against the estimation table. Since $\omega_i$ records the model's confidence that the schema reflects the source text, it can surface a description that is ambiguous, but not one that is internally clear and contradicted elsewhere. Catching the latter requires comparing the schema against the reported results, which is what the test as a whole does. -->

For the remaining four the reported result could not be regenerated from the report, though one of them resists diagnosis: for Team 21, examining both the extracted schema and the generated code turned up nothing that accounts for the gap. The other three reveal reproducibility issues in the reports themselves. Team 9's text names "referee country" as the covariate while the full report shows "player country" is used instead. For Team 27, the authors write that "a variable for player position was included, as well as a variable for the league of the player", which read literally adds only main effects but might equally be shorthand for interactions, consistent with how the other covariates entered their initial model. Team 15 is subtler: their log-linear model includes a skin-tone by league interaction, so the coefficient of interest is defined relative to a parameterization the report does not state, with SPSS's effect coding averaging it across leagues and R's default dummy coding fixing it at a reference league. Setting `contrasts` in R to match recovers the reported value exactly. Neither coding is wrong, but the reported number cannot be regenerated without knowing which one produced it. In all three cases the schema faithfully records what's in the text, and the discrepancy that follows points to a report whose description of the analysis is not precise enough to regenerate the result.

## Exploring alternatives {#sec-explore}

[Im not convinced entirely that this section is necessary - the main gist is to show an exmaple of a branch: multi alternative example. Also I feel leaving the many-analysts football study with the reproducibility issue we identified is a good ending point, and this section is a bit of a tangent. This section is not proofed.]

Team 5 arrives at its final model by comparing three random effect structures, a set of alternative decisions within a single modeling step of the kind described in @sec-alternative. Write $y_{ijm}$ for whether player $i$ received a red card from referee $j$ in game $m$, $x_i$ for player $i$'s skin color rating averaged over the two raters and rescaled to $[0, 1]$, and $c(j)$ for the country of origin of referee $j$. In each model $y_{ijm} \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{ijm})$, and the three differ only in their random effects:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textbf{gm1:} \quad \mathrm{logit}(p_{ijm}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + u_i + v_j, \\
\textbf{gm2:} \quad \mathrm{logit}(p_{ijm}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + u_i + v_{0j} + v_{1j}\, x_i, \\
\textbf{gm3:} \quad \mathrm{logit}(p_{ijm}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + u_i + v_j + w_{0,c(j)} + w_{1,c(j)}\, x_i,
\end{aligned}
$$

with $u_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{player}})$ throughout, $v_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{ref}})$ in gm1 and gm3, $(v_{0j}, v_{1j})^{\top} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{ref}})$ in gm2, and $(w_{0c}, w_{1c})^{\top} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{country}})$ in gm3. Model gm1 lets the baseline log-odds vary across players and referees, gm2 additionally lets the effect of skin color vary across referees, and gm3, the model Team 5 report, instead lets both the baseline and that effect vary across referees' countries of origin.

All three are specified in a single YAML file, following the format described in @sec-alternative and shown in @lst-yaml-alternative. Merging it with Team 5's schema produces one schema per alternative, and each is passed through the same code generation and validation used for the original, yielding three validated scripts from one file and no hand-editing of the team's code. The estimated effect of skin tone is unchanged across this expansion, matching the value Team 5 report and shown for this team in @fig-res-schema.


:::{#lst-yaml-alternative lst-cap="Example of a YAML file specifying alternatives for the random effects structure in the many-analysts analysis of Team 5."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/football-grp5-alt.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Existing reproducible practices focus on whether published results can be reproduced from the code and data, not on the chain of decisions that produced them. We propose a schema that records those decisions along with the rationale for choosing them in natural language as an intermediate representation between the manuscript and the code. A schema can be written by an author or extracted from the manuscript by an LLM. It can then be turned into an executable script, or expanded into a multiverse of alternative analyses. For a published GAITD regression, where the schema was assembled from the manuscript and its supplement, the resulting script reproduced the reported estimates and brought a reviewer's alternative specification within reach of any reader. For the many-analysts football study, where no schema was supplied, extraction and generation recovered most teams' reported effects and identified the few where the methodology could have been described more precisely, inconsistencies that re-running the authors' own code would not reveal. 

A data analysis question admits more than one defensible answer, and the schema records which one was taken. Arriving at those decisions is a matter of human judgement, whether the analyst writes the schema directly or it is extracted from a manuscript in which the decisions were already made. Once they are determined, generating the code is a comparatively mechanical translation, which current LLMs perform with reasonable reliability inside a generation-and-validation loop. Our approach therefore contrasts with fully automated systems that use multiple LLM agents to plan, generate, and execute analyses [@jansen2025; @hu_automated_2024; @sun_lambda_2026], which aim to automate the decisions themselves. @donoho2026 describes the risk in such systems as one of premature autonomy, where the model projects an intent onto the user rather than responding to what was asked. We do not attempt to automate the human judgement that goes into making those decisions, but instead provide a structured way to record them and a workflow to turn them into code.

Three sources of uncertainty enter this pipeline, and they behave differently as models improve. The first is implementation, where the schema states a decision unambiguously and the generated code fails to carry it out: the scripts for Teams 1 and 23 ran and returned estimates after reshaping the data incorrectly. The second is extraction, where the text states a decision clearly to a trained reader and the model fails to recover it. In Team 5's report, the phrase "a random effect of skin tone across referees' countries" is read by most statisticians as implying both a random intercept and a slope, while read literally it specifies only a slope, and the extraction took the literal reading rather than the conventional one. Both are epistemic [@kendall2017; @hullermeier2021] and we would expect them to diminish as models continue to improve, rather than persist as structural limitations of the workflow. The third is aleatoric and belongs to the source text rather than the pipeline: where a report is ambiguous or self-contradictory, as in Teams 9, 27, and 15, no model can recover an intent the text does not express. As extraction and generation improve, what remains is increasingly uncertainty of this third kind, which the schema is designed to make visible.

The validate-and-repair loop assumes that each candidate script can be executed and diagnosed within an interactive timeframe, which rules out analyses too expensive to run repeatedly, and Teams 7, 12, 17, and 18 were excluded on these grounds. Executing such scripts asynchronously through a background job queue would lift the restriction without changing the rest of the workflow.

In our pipeline the model sees the column names but never the values themselves, for privacy reasons. Formats that the schema does not record must therefore be learned through the validation loop. The birth dates in the football data, used to derive player age, are a case in point: the script for Team 21 parsed them as `%Y-%m-%d` and was corrected to `%d.%m.%Y` only after one parse failure, while the repair for Team 1 supplied four candidate formats for R to try in turn. In both cases the date format was recovered by trial and error. When the trials fail, the pipeline can fail outright or carry the failure silently into the analysis.

The implementation reported here is an R package, but nothing about the problem is specific to R, and a general-purpose tool such as a command-line utility would support analyses written in any language. Our implementation records the schema as a single YAML file, which gives the decisions an explicit structure that machines can read. An alternative is to record each decision in its own Markdown file to trade some of that structure for flexibility in how a decision is described. Separate files would further allow decisions to be linked over time, showing how an analysis developed rather than only where it arrived, and with attribution to individual researchers such a history could support a broader research-management system.
